analysis.one_liner: Gives every voter $100 in public campaign vouchers to give to federal candidates who accept small-donation limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Rules Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Elections Act would give every eligible adult voter $100 in "democracy dollars" for each federal election — House, Senate, and presidential — to hand to candidates of their choice, with the government paying the candidate for the vouchers. Candidates who join the program would have to raise a minimum in small donations first, cap the size of individual contributions (shrinking to $200 over time), and spend almost none of their own money. It would also repeal the existing presidential public financing system. The bill is in its first step: introduced and sent to the Senate Rules Committee, with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who cannot afford large political donations — the bill hands each of them $100 per election to direct to candidates, and directs outreach to people who have never given to a campaign. It also benefits candidates who currently struggle to compete against opponents funded by big donors: once they certify, small-dollar and voucher money becomes their main funding source, and contribution limits phase down to $200 per donor. Under the program, campaign money in participating races would come mostly from voters rather than a small class of maximum donors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who don't make political donations

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible adult who is registered (where registration is required) can request $100 in democracy dollars per election for House, Senate, and presidential races, and direct it to any certified participating candidate.

Candidates who join the program must phase down the individual contributions they accept — from $1,000 in 2029 to $200 by 2037 — and may spend no more than $2,500 of their own money, which makes small donors the dominant source of campaign funds for participating campaigns.

Candidates must raise a floor in small donations first ($50,000 for House, $500,000 for Senate, $1 million for president) before receiving voucher money, and the FEC is directed to run outreach targeted at people who have never contributed to a campaign before.
Voucher transfers count as the voter's own contribution and are reported with the voter's name protected, so participation does not put a voter on a public donor list.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the vouchers — the bill appropriates "such sums as necessary," so the cost scales with how many voters claim their $100 and is not capped. Wealthy donors and self-funding candidates lose the ability to dominate participating candidates' funding: their contribution limit to those candidates phases down to $200, and participating candidates may not spend more than $2,500 of their own money. Existing presidential public financing (the tax checkoff fund) is repealed, with leftover money moved to the general Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as necessary' with no cost cap, and the amounts must be indexed upward if private fundraising outpaces voucher use — an open-ended federal spending commitment for elections.

Participating candidates may spend no more than $2,500 of their own (or their immediate family's) money across an entire election series, which could put a wealthy self-funded opponent who refuses to participate at a structural advantage.

The bill repeals the existing presidential public financing system — including the income tax checkoff that funds it — and sweeps leftover Presidential Election Campaign Fund money into the general Treasury, replacing one program with an untested one.

The program depends on the Federal Election Commission to build the distribution, audit, and privacy systems, and Section 506 puts voucher payments in line only up to the amount actually appropriated, with later-transferred vouchers paid out of order once funds run short.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large — reducing the role of concentrated private money in federal elections and letting every voter fund candidates with $100 of public money [S2] — but the design has real drawbacks. The open-ended appropriation could cost tens of billions per two-year cycle, the $2,500 personal-fund cap could hurt participating candidates against self-funded opponents, and repealing the existing presidential financing system eliminates one program before the replacement has proved itself [S2]. The bill also relies on the FEC to build the entire voucher system from scratch. On the merits it is a genuine attempt to shift campaign funding toward ordinary voters, with costs and design risks an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Rules Committee, and — with no cosponsors — has sat there without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the Clean Elections Act in the Senate on August 6, 2026.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, the committee that handles election law.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded.

The bill's substance would create a 'Democracy Dollars' program giving eligible voters $100 in vouchers per election to give to certified candidates, who in exchange would accept phased-down contribution limits and a $2,500 cap on personal spending, and it would repeal the existing presidential public financing system, effective after 2028.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the outcome preserves the current campaign finance system: large donors and self-funding candidates keep the influence they have under existing law, and no taxpayer money is spent. Nothing has been lost yet, but nothing has changed either.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 6, 2026 and spoke for it as its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 6, 2026 and has taken no action on the bill since.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, is attached to the bill, so no partisan pattern has formed; no Republican and no other Democrat has cosponsored it [S3].

industries.industry: Large political donors and wealthy self-funders
industries.note: For any candidate in the program, individual contribution limits phase down to $200 and personal spending is capped at $2,500, shrinking the leverage of donors who now give the maximum or bankroll their own campaigns. Wealthy candidates who decline to participate are untouched.

industries.industry: Political advertising, media, and campaign consulting
industries.note: Federal voucher money adds a new stream of campaign spending on top of existing contributions, and campaign spending flows heavily into advertising and consulting. Their interest runs alongside voters' only insofar as more money circulates; they do not bear the program's cost.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a single-sponsor measure with zero cosponsors, referred late in a two-year Congress to the Rules and Administration Committee, which has not acted on it. Most bills at this stage die quietly when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Advancing would require the committee to hold a hearing and mark it up and the Senate to schedule floor time — steps that, on this record, show no signs of happening.
